title: A galactic maelstrom
caption: Spiral galaxy Messier 96, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 96, NGC 3368 · constellation Leo · about 35 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA and the LEGUS Team Acknowledgement: R. Gendler

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Glowing gas swirls through this Hubble view of Messier 96 like a giant maelstrom, rippled with dark dust that spirals in toward the nucleus. The spiral galaxy lies just over 35 million light-years away in Leo, the Lion, and is roughly as massive and as large as our own Milky Way.

On closer inspection Messier 96 is lopsided. Its gas and dust are spread unevenly through weak spiral arms, the arms themselves are asymmetrical, and even its core is slightly off the galaxy's center. Astronomers think its lopsided arms were shaped by the gravity of other galaxies in its group.

That group, the M96 Group, also contains the bright galaxies Messier 105 and Messier 95, along with a number of smaller, fainter members. It is the nearest group to contain bright spirals as well as a bright elliptical, which is Messier 105.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.73 x 2.79 arcminutes) and distance (35 million light years), the frame spans roughly 28,000 × 28,000 light-years. Its light set out about 35 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using blue, green and near-infrared filters. The color assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, beyond human vision, and the long exposure gathers far more light than an eye could.

explore: Pierre Méchain discovered the galaxy in 1781, and Charles Messier added it to his famous catalog of astronomical objects only four days later.
alt: A spiral galaxy of glowing gas streaked with dark dust swirling in toward its nucleus.
